newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish Senate passes bill to vet officials' past.
newsitem.headline: Polish Senate passes bill to vet officials' past.

text.p: Poland's Senate passed a bill on Thursday that would allow applicants for senior public posts to be screened for possible ties with communist-era security police.
The Senate voted 47 to 33 with one abstention for the bill, which now only requires President Aleksander Kwasniewski's signature to become law.

Under the bill those seeking elected posts and senior positions in the government, judiciary or media, would have to openly declare whether they had been informants for the security police under communism.

Unlike some former Soviet bloc countries, Poland has not opened the communist security police files and the issue, long part of political campaigning, is expected also to play a role in this year's general elections due around September.
Supporters of vetting say former agents of the SB security service have taken important state jobs and are now vulnerable to blackmail.
Others, notably ex-communists, argue it is too late to start opening files and that the archives are too unreliable to allow a fair vetting.
But they were defeated in the lower house by the joint forces of the opposition and their own coalition partners from the Peasant party.
Kwasniewski, himself an ex-communist, has signalled he might veto the bill.
He said that while he supported it in principle, the bill's proposal also to screen collaborators of the communist era intelligence and counter-intelligence services could threaten state security.
